pr_title: sd-id128: make sd_id128_get_machine() return -ENOMEDIUM when not initialized
pr_body:
At least, bootctl and sd-journal has special handling about -ENOMEDIUM, but previously these are not correctly triggered.

Fixes #25634.
pr_comments:
Hmm, is this right?

See machine-id(5) man page, the part about "first boot semantics".

1. /etc/machine-id empty means "not first boot, but overmount/persist machine ID acquired elsewhere"

2. /etc/machine-id containing "uninitialized" means "first boot, persist/overmount machine ID"

3. /etc/machine-id missing is same as containing string "uninitialized"

So far sd_id128_get_machine() returned ENOMEDIUM in case of case 1, and EINVAL in case of 2, and ENOENT in case of 3.

with your patch the you also return ENOMEDIUM in case of 2. Which I think is probably not what should be happening, given that this makes these two cases indistinguishable. But they are big time different.

I guess log_execution_mode() in src/main.c should use sd_id128_get_machine() btw, to detect first boot mode, currently i reads the ID manually...

It appears to me we probably should:

1. Get rid of ID128_PLAIN_OR_UNINIT
2. Ensure/document to always return ENOMEDIUM in case of empty /etc/machine-id
3. Ensure/document to always return ENOPKG (or some other new errno) in case of /etc/machine-id containing "uninitialized"
4. Ensure/document to always return ENOENT in case of missing /etc/machine-id
5. Port all logic that checks /etc/machine-id for firstboot/initialization to actually use sd_id128_get_machine(), and look at the error code.
6. Be careful about caching the read id: only cash if we actually managed to read an ID, and in case of ENOMEDIUM/ENOPKG/ENOENT ensure we don#t cache, but when the id is requested again we'll got to disk again (this might already be what happens)
7. I think the caching currently trats the id128 of all zeroes specially. to avoid confusion, if we manage to read an id from disk, maybe we should return EINVAL if it is SD_ID128_NULL or SD_ID128_ALLF...
@poettering Thank you for the detailed suggestion. Hopefully addressed. PTAL!

```

```
Thank you for the review. Updated. PTAL.

issue_context.title: bootctl install fails when `/etc/machine-id` is set to `uninitialized`
issue_context.body:
### systemd version the issue has been seen with

252

### Used distribution

Debian 12

### Linux kernel version used

5.19.0-2-amd64

### CPU architectures issue was seen on

x86_64

### Component

bootctl

### Expected behaviour you didn't see

`bootctl install` completes without error

### Unexpected behaviour you saw

It outputs
```
Failed to get machine-id: Invalid argument
```
and exits with `1`

I think this because in [sd-id128.c](https://github.com/systemd/systemd/blob/main/src/libsystemd/sd-id128/sd-id128.c#L126) the type is `ID128_PLAIN` instead of `ID128_PLAIN_OR_UNINIT`. [This](https://github.com/systemd/systemd/blob/main/src/boot/bootctl.c#L181) should be the relevant call in bootctl.

### Steps to reproduce the problem

```
echo "uninitialized" > /etc/machine-id
bootctl install
```

### Additional program output to the terminal or log subsystem illustrating the issue

```sh
The debug output is

No filesystem is currently mounted on /sys/fs/cgroup.
Failed to detect cgroup namespace: No medium found
Found container virtualization none.
File system "/boot" is not a FAT EFI System Partition (ESP) file system.
Using EFI System Partition at /boot/efi.
Directory "/boot" is not the root of the file system.
Didn't find an XBOOTLDR partition, using the ESP as $BOOT.
Failed to get machine-id: Invalid argument
```
```

review_comments: maybe add a test here that only one of the two flags are set?
